evidence.claim: Between Durango and Chama, a border drive follows narrow-gauge railroad history
evidence.quote: The Tracks Across Borders Byway is along the Colorado and New Mexico border between Durango, Colorado and Chama, New Mexico.

evidence.claim: a border drive follows narrow-gauge railroad history
evidence.quote: The Byway’s primary feature is one of Colorado’s greatest stories - the creation and development of the state’s first, and ultimately the nation’s largest, narrow gauge railroad system - the Denver and Rio Grande Railroad (D&RG).

evidence.claim: Tracks Across Borders runs between Durango and Chama along the Colorado–New Mexico border, crossing Southern Ute Indian Tribe reservation land and skirting Navajo Lake’s northern end.
evidence.quote: The Byway passes through the Southern Ute Indian Tribe reservation land, whose headquarters and superlative Southern Ute Cultural Center and Museum are located in Ignacio, Colorado. The Byway skirts the north end of Navajo Lake

evidence.claim: Colorado DOT gives the full drive as 125 miles and four and a half hours.
evidence.quote: 125 miles total CO/NM, time 4 1/2 hours

evidence.claim: In its scenic-byways program, the agency identifies the Denver and Rio Grande narrow-gauge railroad as the route’s principal story.
evidence.quote: The Byway’s primary feature is one of Colorado’s greatest stories - the creation and development of the state’s first, and ultimately the nation’s largest, narrow gauge railroad system - the Denver and Rio Grande Railroad (D&RG).

evidence.claim: The railroad’s San Juan Extension was built to reach the mineral resources near Silverton.
evidence.quote: The purpose of this extension was to tap into the mineral resources around the Silverton, Colorado area.

evidence.claim: Three-foot track cost less to build and accommodated tighter curves than standard gauge.
evidence.quote: This was because narrow gauge was cheaper to build, and narrow gauge railways can accommodate tighter-radius curves.

evidence.claim: Crews reached Chama on December 31, 1880, then continued toward Durango.
evidence.quote: From Antonito, the line continued west to Chama, New Mexico, arriving there on December 31, 1880.

evidence.claim: The Durango–Chama tracks were later removed, while the Durango–Silverton branch survived.
evidence.quote: the tracks from Durango east to Chama, New Mexico, and south to Farmington, New Mexico, were removed, but the Silverton Branch remained in operation

evidence.claim: From Durango, the journey reaches Ignacio, home to the Tribe’s headquarters and cultural center and museum.
evidence.quote: The Byway passes through the Southern Ute Indian Tribe reservation land, whose headquarters and superlative Southern Ute Cultural Center and Museum are located in Ignacio, Colorado.

evidence.claim: At Arboles, the Piedra River enters Navajo Reservoir near the state line.
evidence.quote: It enters Navajo Reservoir near the town of Arboles, near the New Mexico state line.

evidence.claim: The route includes a round-trip spur to Chimney Rock National Monument.
evidence.quote: Chimney Rock National Monument is an essential thematic feature of national significance on the Byway. The round-trip spur provides access

evidence.claim: The road journey ends at Chama, western terminus of the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad, whose preserved line continues toward Antonito.
evidence.quote: Chama is now the western terminus of the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad, a steam-driven, narrow gauge heritage railway which carries visitors to and from Osier, Colorado, and Antonito, Colorado, during the summer months.

evidence.claim: Three-foot track
evidence.quote: The company chose the narrow gauge of three feet

evidence.claim: then continued toward Durango
evidence.quote: The line then went on towards Durango, Colorado.

evidence.claim: Ignacio is home to the Southern Ute Indian Tribe’s headquarters and the Southern Ute Cultural Center and Museum.
evidence.quote: whose headquarters and superlative Southern Ute Cultural Center and Museum are located in Ignacio, Colorado.

evidence.claim: Its Ute name is Piinuu.
evidence.quote: Ignacio (Ute dialect: Piinuu)

evidence.claim: The town lies within a history of shrinking reservation boundaries: the Brunot Treaty removed the San Juan Mountains from the Consolidated Ute Reservation in 1873.
evidence.quote: On September 13, 1873, the Brunot Treaty removed the San Juan Mountains from the Consolidated Ute Reservation.

evidence.claim: In 1878, that reservation was replaced by the much smaller Southern Ute Indian Reservation.
evidence.quote: On November 9, 1878, the Consolidated Ute Reservation was replaced by the much smaller Southern Ute Indian Reservation.

evidence.claim: Ignacio’s post office opened in 1882; incorporation followed in 1913.
evidence.quote:
The Ignacio, Colorado, post office opened on Jan 31, 1882
The Town of Ignacio was incorporated on July 7, 1913.

evidence.claim: The Piedra River’s meeting with the San Juan lies beneath Navajo Reservoir.
evidence.quote: Its confluence with the San Juan River, inside Navajo State Park, is drowned under the waters of the reservoir.

evidence.claim: The Piedra enters the reservoir near Arboles, whose name means trees in Spanish.
evidence.quote: It enters Navajo Reservoir near the town of Arboles, near the New Mexico state line.

evidence.claim: Navajo Dam was completed in 1962.
evidence.quote: Navajo Dam, 3,800 feet (1,200 m) long and 400 feet (120 m) high, completed in 1962.

evidence.claim: The rising water displaced families from Los Arboles, Los Pinos, Rose and Los Martinez.
evidence.quote: The waters of Navajo Lake forced hundreds of families to leave their homes and communities. The four communities affected were Los Arboles, Los Pinos, Rose and Los Martinez.

evidence.claim: The reservoir stores and releases San Juan River water for local irrigation and the Colorado River downstream.
evidence.quote: manages the upper reaches of the San Juan River, storing and releasing water that is used locally for irrigation, or ultimately reaching the Colorado River in Utah.

evidence.claim: Its Colorado shoreline is part of Navajo State Park.
evidence.quote: the Portion of the shoreline and portion of the lake that is located in Colorado make up Navajo State Park

evidence.claim: whose name means trees in Spanish
evidence.quote: The town's name means "trees" in Spanish.

evidence.claim: A sandstone ridge leads toward Chimney Rock, with Companion Rock beside it.
evidence.quote: The primary settlements that have been excavated lie on the ridge that eventually terminates at Chimney Rock. The ridge is mostly bedrock made of sandstone.

evidence.claim: The Great House Pueblo has 36 rooms and two kivas, or round ceremonial rooms.
evidence.quote: It consists of 36 rooms and two kivas.

evidence.claim: Evidence suggests construction began in 1076 during a lunar standstill and expansion followed during another in 1093.
evidence.quote: Evidence suggests that Great House Pueblo was first built in AD 1076 during a lunar standstill and expanded and finished in AD 1093 during another.

evidence.claim: Building materials were carried by hand up the ridge from below.
evidence.quote: Material to build the Great House Pueblo came from downhill and was hauled by hand up the ridge line from further below.

evidence.claim: The archaeological site became a national monument in 2012.
evidence.quote: U.S. President Barack Obama created Chimney Rock National Monument by proclamation on September 21, 2012, under authority of the Antiquities Act.

evidence.claim: with Companion Rock beside it
evidence.quote: Next to Chimney Rock is Companion Rock

evidence.claim: kivas, or round ceremonial rooms
evidence.quote: round ceremonial rooms, known as kivas

evidence.claim: CDOT advises against the central section south of Pagosa Junction/Juanita in inclement or severe weather. Its detour follows CR 500 north to Pagosa Springs, then US 160 east and US 84 south toward Dulce or Chama.
evidence.quote: Travel in inclement weather or during severe weather conditions is not advised for the small central section of the byway south of Pagosa Junction/Juanita. A convenient detour over a well-maintained county road from Pagosa Junction is north on Trujillo Road (CR 500) to Pagosa Springs, continuing east on Highway 160 to Highway 84, then south to Dulce or Chama.

evidence.claim: Colorado and New Mexico bought the Chama–Antonito line, and the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad formed by 1971. Those states have jointly owned the surviving line since 1970.
evidence.quote: the line has been jointly owned by the states of Colorado and New Mexico since 1970.

evidence.claim: the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad formed by 1971
evidence.quote: by 1971, the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad was formed.

evidence.claim: The park uplands have flat-topped mesas and rolling hills cut in places by steep-sided canyons. Pinyon-juniper woodland occupies dry slopes, hills and mesa tops.
evidence.quote: Uplands within the park are characterized by flat-topped mesas and gently rolling hills, occasionally cut by steep-sided canyons.

evidence.claim: Pinyon-juniper woodland occupies dry slopes, hills and mesa tops.
evidence.quote: comprise the pinyon-juniper woodland community, occupying dry slopes, hills and mesa tops.

evidence.claim: The trail to the Great House begins beside a complex of three pit houses and workrooms. Excavated workrooms contained separate areas with stones for grinding corn.
evidence.quote: The base of the trail up to Great House Pueblo begins next to a pit-house complex made up of three pit houses and accompanying workrooms.

evidence.claim: Excavated workrooms contained separate areas with stones for grinding corn.
evidence.quote: Excavations of the workrooms showed separate areas with grinding stones for corn

evidence.claim: The route includes a round-trip spur to Chimney Rock National Monument.
evidence.quote: Chimney Rock National Monument is an essential thematic feature of national significance on the Byway. The round-trip spur provides access

evidence.claim: Peregrine falcons nest each year on Companion Rock.
evidence.quote: Peregrine falcons continue to nest in Companion Rock each year.

evidence.claim: Colorado and New Mexico bought the Chama–Antonito line
evidence.quote: In April 1969, legislation was signed in New Mexico that authorized the state to purchase the track between Chama and Antonito. In 1970, Colorado passed similar legislation. The two states jointly owned the line

Omitted the current almost-200-family displacement count because the cache calls it an estimate and also says hundreds; retained the affected communities without an unresolved total.
Rail abandonment dates conflict: Chama says September 1967; Durango describes freight ending in 1968; the railroad article dates an abandonment filing to September 1968. Exact date omitted.
No tribal-authored history or monument-manager access page is cached. Ignacio is short to avoid expanding beyond the available evidence; no ceremony or museum admission promise is made.
Strip mileages reset before Pagosa Junction and omit Chama; retained stops follow Ignacio–Arboles order, with Chimney Rock explicitly a separate excursion.
Top-level practical object carries the essential CDOT weather detour; the supplied output example omits this field but the route itself requires it.
CDOT gives duration and lakeside character but little detail on road surface, curves or grades.
